88fits / design bible

Drag to run. The guns aim themselves. A portrait, third-person survivor-shooter in the Megabonk mould: clean anime-styled heroes in a painted desert on 3D ground, a few dozen creatures on screen, level-ups that hand you three cards, chests that spin a reel, poison and fire builds that never mix, structures worth crossing the map for, and a meta that keeps you unlocking between runs.

version 0.9 date 2026-09-17 status playable, iterated from the phone engine Godot 4.7.2
How to read this

This is a description of the game as it is built, not a plan. Every number is the number in the content files, every screenshot is a capture from the current build, and every creature and item pictured was painted by the art pipeline in section 15. Where a rule was tried and dropped, the section says so in one line and moves on. Earlier versions kept a changelog at the top; this one folds everything into the sections and keeps a short history in section 18.

01

Vision & pillars

The question this project answers: does a Megabonk-style run work in portrait with one thumb? The build says yes. What follows is the game that answer became, and the rules that keep it growing without turning into code.

The pitch in three sentences

You are a small goofy hero in a very big, very hot desert, and the desert hates you. Goblins, roadrunners, fire ants, spitting cacti, mummies and beetles pour in from every side while your weapons fire on their own, so your only job is to steer through the mess, hoover up XP gems, find the structures scattered over the map, and pick the best card every time you level up. Survive the boss, walk into the portal, and decide whether to bank your gold or push into a harder stage.

One thumb, zero menus

Every in-run action is hold, slide, or tap. If a feature needs a second finger or a button cluster, it is cut or automated.

Portrait is the point

The tall screen shows more ahead than beside. Threat comes from the front and steering is the skill. We design around it, not despite it.

Cards go brr

Vampire Survivors weapon stacking: six weapons, six passives, evolutions. Runs feel different because builds feel different.

A crowd, not a queue

Two dozen creatures on screen from minute one, sixty by the end, every one of them a little different. The screen should look like a problem you can read.

Goofy and readable

Anime-style sprites for characters (crisp line art, cel shading, flat saturated colours), real 3D for weapons, pickups and the world. Silly on purpose, clear at a glance on a phone.

Content is data

A new weapon, passive, creature, structure or pickup is a new folder, never new code, and it is visible and editable inside the Godot editor. See section 14.

What it is not

  • Not a parkour game. Jumps happen automatically at marked ledges and pads. There is no jump button.
  • Not an aiming game. No crosshair, no manual fire. Facing still matters for cone weapons, which gives steering a combat purpose.
  • Not a shop-between-waves game like Brotato. Progression inside a run is the starter pick, level-up cards, chests, and whatever structures you reach.
02

Reference games

Each reference is named for one thing we borrow, so later we can say "Archero-style cards" or "Megabonk-style portal" and both know exactly what is meant.

Megabonk

3D · third person · goofy

We take
Tone and humour. Stages ending in a boss and a portal. Extract-or-continue tension. Characters and items unlocked by completing in-run challenges. Permanent upgrade shop between runs. 3D pickups and weapon effects around a flat character. Landmarks on the map that are worth a detour.
We skip
Parkour, wall jumps, manual jumping, landscape framing.

Vampire Survivors

2D · the genre template

We take
Auto-firing weapons. Six weapon slots plus six passive slots. Weapon levels to 8. Evolution by pairing a max weapon with its passive. XP gems and magnet. Pick 1 of 3 on level up. Reroll, skip and banish as meta unlocks. The pause screen that lists every item you hold. Chests that spin before they reveal.
We skip
The 30-minute timer, the arcana system, the sheer item count for now.

Archero

portrait · one thumb · mobile pacing

We take
Portrait HUD conventions. Full-screen level-up cards sized for thumbs. Chapter pacing where a run is 10 to 15 minutes with bosses on a schedule. A title screen that is one big PLAY button.
We skip
Stop-to-shoot. Rooms and doors. Equipment gacha.

Brotato

starter choice · stat transparency

We take
Picking a starting weapon before the run. A stats screen that shows every number with where it came from.
We skip
Shop between waves, discrete waves, top-down 2D.

Survivor.io

portrait Vampire Survivors

We take
Proof that the genre reads fine in portrait. The slim top strip with timer and item rows, the round pause button, the navy-and-gold look of the menus. The floating joystick and the camera that never rotates: the scheme that shipped.
We skip
Monetisation layers.

The one idea without a reference, hold-to-run, slide-to-steer, was the feel test's hypothesis. It lost to the joystick on the first phone session and section 04 records why.

03

The screen

The HUD is a thin strip over the world, Survivor.io's proportion: everything below it belongs to the thumb. Whatever must be read mid-fight sits either in that strip or on the ground next to the hero.

HUD anatomy

top strip
250 px of 1920, 13% of the screen. Row one: LV badge, XP bar, stage name. Row two: kills and alive count left, the timer big in the middle, gold right. Row three: the twelve item slots. A gradient that fades into the world, no panel, every piece of text outlined so it reads over sand and sky. Tapping the strip pauses.
slots
Six weapon squares on the left, six passive circles on the right, 72 px each, a level badge in the corner that turns gold at max level. Empty slots are faint outlines. Same icon files as the cards and the pause screen.
pause
A round gold button at the right end of the strip, where Survivor.io keeps it. Two bars drawn as shapes, so no font can break it.
buffs
A row of chips under the strip while a timed effect runs (Rage, Sprint, Shield, the War Drum), each with its seconds left.
on the player
Health bar under the character, not in the HUD. It is a pair of quads in the world attached to the hero, not a HUD element projected each frame, so it moves in the same frame as the sprite and never trails it. It disappears when the hero is down.
XP
Gems collected within a quarter second are batched into one rising "+N XP" label over the hero and the bar pops, so a sweep through a gem field reads as one reward, not forty.
boss
BOSS IN 0:45 counts down just under the strip in the last 45 s (banner at 30, pulse under 10); the boss name and bar take the same spot while a boss is alive.
where the big one is
Whenever the boss or the Elite is alive and off screen, a chevron at the screen edge points at it with its name and distance ("BOSS 42 m"), red for the boss, orange for the Elite. It disappears the moment the creature is in view, so it never covers a fight.
thumb zone
Everything below the strip, 86% of the screen. A faint ring appears where the thumb lands and fades after a second. Nothing is ever drawn here that needs reading.
safe areas
HUD respects the notch and gesture bar insets from the OS. Gameplay renders edge to edge.
04

Controls

The whole game is one thumb on the lower two thirds of the screen: a floating joystick, the scheme every portrait survivor game settled on (Archero, Survivor.io, Vampire Survivors mobile). Touch anywhere, the stick appears under the thumb, drag to run in that direction, lift to stop.

The rules of the thumb

touch down
The joystick base appears under the thumb, anywhere below the top bar. No fixed position to find, no acceleration ramp: the first frame of drag already moves.
drag
Direction of the stick = direction of travel on screen (north is up, because the camera never turns). Dead zone 6 px. Throttle ramps to full speed at about half deflection, so a small nudge creeps through a gap and a full push sprints. The hero faces where they run.
long drag
Past the rim the base trails the thumb, so a thumb that wandered keeps steering from where it is. Joystick size is a slider in settings (0.6 to 1.4).
lift
Stop on the spot. Standing still is a legitimate tactic. Weapons keep firing.
auto-fire
Every weapon fires on its own cooldown and aims itself: nearest, random, the thickest crowd, the nearest healthy creature for poison, or a cone pointed at the nearest creature (the shotgun family), so shots always leave towards something. The facing only decides where the held gun points when nothing is in range. Every hit pushes: each weapon carries a knockback stat (metres per second of shove on a 1 m creature; heavier creatures budge less, the boss barely).
stand to use
Structures are used by standing inside their ring for three seconds; the progress fills on the ground. Walking out drains it. Chests and pickups are used by walking over them.
auto-jump
Running off a marked ledge or onto a jump pad triggers a fixed arc. The player cannot fall off the map. Raised paths hold chests and shortcuts.
tap a card
Level-up, starter choice, the chest's Take or Sell, the shop's three items. Big targets, no drag, no confirm step.
pause
The round gold button at the right end of the HUD strip (tapping the strip works too). Full build and stats readout, options, abandon run. See section 12.
keyboard, PC only
WASD or the arrow keys move the hero exactly like a full stick push; no ring is drawn. The four actions (move_left/right/up/down) live in the project's Input Map, so they can be rebound in the editor without code. Escape pauses, or closes the shop. Phones never see them.
reserved
Double-tap dash and a second-thumb ability button are ideas for later.
What the feel test found

The first scheme was hold-to-run, slide-to-steer, with the camera behind the hero. Turning the character was a chore, not a decision: the thumb fought the rotating camera and every dodge needed a two-step steer. The joystick makes a dodge one motion, the way the benchmark games do it, and leaves the decisions to positioning, which is where this genre keeps them.

05

Camera

A fixed camera, north always up, the way Archero and Survivor.io frame the fight: the world never rotates, so the stick maps straight to the screen and the map stays learnable. It is bolted to the hero: no lead, no lag, so the stick never feels like it is also steering the view. Only hits shake it.

fixed (default)
Yaw locked to north, position locked to a point north of the hero, so they stand a little below the screen centre and see more of what is coming. Screen shake on every hit the hero takes (and on evolutions, big explosions and boss slams). The hero sprite switches between back, back-diagonal, side, front-diagonal and front views from the direction of travel, diagonals mirrored, eight directions in all.
follow (option)
Yaw follows the hero's facing with a short lag and a dead zone so turns feel weighty; the hero is seen from behind. Switch in Options at any time, even mid-run.
aspect
Keep-height projection. Every phone sees the same distance ahead. Wider phones see a bit more to the sides.
terrain
The camera rides the terrain height under the player, smoothed, so dunes and the riverbed do not bounce the view. Mesa tops raise the camera with the player.
readability
Creatures far up the screen are small. The Elite is three times a goblin's height and the boss five, so they read at distance; the edge pointer covers the rest.
06

Dry Gulch

One map, the golden-hour desert. It is not a plane: gentle dunes, a sunken dry riverbed, two sandstone mesas you auto-jump between, and enough oversized scenery that steering means something. The ground, the mesas and the landmarks (gas station, water tower, wrecked pickup, the structures) are 3D; the scenery itself is painted: cacti, agaves, dead trees, rocks, skulls and bones are 2.5D sprites in the same anime line as the cast, scattered over the terrain by a seeded roll. A second map (a meadow) was built in an earlier pass and has been shelved to keep the focus on making one map excellent; its files are backed up and it will come back as a content pack.

Theme rules

time of day
Golden hour, always. Warm orange light from one side, long soft shadows baked into props, purple sky at the top. It flatters painted sprites and hides low polygon counts.
skybox
A panorama: gradient from dusk purple to orange, a big low sun, a far ring of mesa silhouettes, three lazy clouds. The sun is also the directional light.
ground
A 140 m heightmap terrain, not a plane. Dunes of about ±1.5 m, the riverbed 2 m lower with a cracked-earth texture, sand elsewhere. Two textures blended by height, low-frequency path noise so the blend never looks like camouflage.
walls
A ring of modular mesa blocks. The camera never sees past them, so the world ends without a visible edge.
scenery
Fourteen painted props (art/sprites/props/): saguaros big and small, barrel cactus, prickly pear, agave, dead shrub, dead tree, three sizes of sandstone rock, a cow skull, a small skull, a bone pile and a signpost. Sixteen greenery clusters (a big saguaro with three to six smaller plants round it), ten rock groups, six lone dead trees, twenty-two bones and three signposts, never on the flats, the riverbed, a mesa or a landmark. Cacti, trees, rocks and signs collide (a cylinder under each); bones do not. The 3D landmarks stay: the wrecked pickup, the gas station, the water tower, the wind pump, the campfire, tumbleweeds, and the seven structure props.
moving bits
Tumbleweeds roll through on the wind and bounce off things, riding the terrain instead of sinking through it. One dust devil roams and throws creatures and hero alike. The greenery sways: each plant's top leans a few degrees back and forth in the vertex shader, the base stays put.
scale joke
The hero is small. Cacti are twice their height, the pickup is a building, the skull is a bench. Oversized props sell the goofy tone and the third-person camera.
lighting budget
One directional light, no real-time shadows on mobile, ambient from the sky colour, a fake blob shadow under every character. Campfire, structures and the portal get a single omni light each.

Blender's role

  • Landmarks and structures. The gas station, water tower, pickup, campfire, tumbleweed and the seven structure props are modelled low-poly in Blender by script (tools/blender_props.py), given flat painted materials and exported as GLB into res://art/props. The scenery is not Blender's any more: see section 15.
  • Weapon meshes. Saw blades, the shotgun, grenades, the turret, the pea pod and the dart familiars, the gem, the coin, the chest, the portal ring. Small, chunky, built in the scene files.
  • Not Blender. Characters and creatures are 2D painted sprites. Blender only ever renders their pose skeletons (section 15).
07

The run

A run is 15 minutes in three 5-minute stages. It opens with a starter weapon pick. Each stage ends with a boss and a portal; halfway to each boss an Elite shows up. Walk through the portal to bank your gold with a bonus, or stay and face a harder stage. Death also ends the run and keeps what you earned.

Run rules

starter pick
Before the timer starts, three weapon cards. See section 11. The chosen weapon goes into slot 1 at level 1.
length
15 minutes for a full clear, benchmarked on Archero's early chapters and Survivor.io stages. Short enough for a bus ride, long enough for a build to come online.
stages
Three per map. The stage timer drives the wave director. Each stage raises the difficulty multiplier, the live cap and creature speed, and the boss comes back twice as tough. Stage 2 should feel like a wall to a build that coasted through stage 1.
the Elite
Halfway to every boss (2:30, 7:30, 12:30, and every 150 s after a boss in endless) a mini-boss appears near the hero with nothing but a toast: no bar, no phase change, regular spawning carries on. On Dry Gulch it is the Dune Scorpion: a charger three times a goblin's height with 260 HP that scales ×1.8 per stage. It always drops a chest, and the HUD points at it while it lives.
boss
At the end of every stage, on the flats. Big silhouette, three telegraphed attacks, a bar under the HUD strip, and a chest where it dies. Regular spawning slows to a trickle while the boss lives.
portal
Appears where the boss dies. Extract banks gold at ×1.25 and ends the run. Continue starts the next stage. After stage 3, an endless mode continues with the multiplier climbing every minute.
death
Ends the run. All gold collected is kept at ×1.0. A revive is a meta unlock, one per run. The hero lies still and the health bar goes away.
spawning
Continuous, not discrete waves. A live cap grows with time. When the cap has room, the director spawns from the current roster on a ring outside the view, mostly ahead of the hero, in bursts of 2 to 6 packs so groups arrive as groups.

Chests and the reel

who drops them
Every elite variant and the Elite always. Every boss. Regular creatures rarely, by a chest chance in their drop table: a goblin one time in 500, a mummy one in 100, a beetle one in 67, so a full run sees two or three from the crowd. The Dice Shrine's ambush leaves one as consolation.
what they hold
Decided before the reel spins: an evolution if any weapon is maxed with its passive held, otherwise one level of a random owned item that can still grow, otherwise 50 gold. The reel is honest: the result is fixed when the chest opens and the spin is the reveal.
selling
A fifth of what the travelling shop would charge (section 07, structures), so a common item's level fetches two or three gold and an epic evolution six. Small on purpose: the point is the choice, not the income. Gold has no Sell button.
pause
The reel runs on the paused game like the card screen does; a pending level-up waits until the chest is closed.

Structures

Seven small landmarks are scattered over the map at run start, one of every kind, at least 22 m apart. Each is single use: stand inside its ring and a wedge fills on the ground over three seconds (a dark hand on its leading edge, so it reads on any ground); step out and it drains. Used structures go grey.

StructureWeightWhat it does
Healing WellCold water. Warm feeling.4Heals half of max HP.
Loot CacheSomebody buried this. Somebody was wrong.340 gold, three large gems and a handful of coins.
XP BeaconA crystal humming with someone else's experience.3An instant level-up.
Travelling ShopThree things for sale. Buy one, then it packs up.2Three random items from the level-up pool with prices by power: a common item 12 gold, rare 20, epic 32, a quarter more per level already held, passives a fifth cheaper. Buy one with run gold and the stall packs up; a close button and "Leave without buying" are always there.
War DrumHit it. Then hit everything else.2+50% might and +25% area for 30 s.
Dice ShrineFull heal, a pile of gold, a level, or an ambush.2One of: full heal, 150 gold, a level-up, or a ring of the map's swarmers with a chest as consolation.
Uber MagnetEvery gem and coin on the map comes home. Once.1Every gem and coin on the ground flies to the hero.

Each structure is a folder under content/structures/ (effect kind, numbers, weight, colour, which Blender prop); the map's timeline says how many and how far apart. New kinds need a folder and, for a new effect, one more branch in Game.use_structure.

Pickups

Every 55 to 95 seconds (the first after 50) a pickup appears a short run from the hero and waits twenty seconds, blinking at the end: a Heart (30% of max HP), Rage (+50% might for 20 s), Sprint (+40% speed, faster cooldowns, 15 s), a Shield (no damage for 6 s, the hero tinted blue) or a Magnet Pulse (every gem on the map comes home). They are never pulled by the magnet: you walk to them, through whatever is in the way. Hearts are the common one; the run stays hard because they are rare, short and somewhere else. Each is a folder under content/pickups/ and the map's timeline says which ones it offers and how often.

08

Weapons, passives & evolutions

Pure Vampire Survivors: six weapon slots, six passive slots, every weapon levels to 8, and a maxed weapon plus its paired passive evolves at the next chest. Thirteen weapons, eleven passives, thirteen evolutions. Every weapon is a 3D object in the world, because saw blades, grenades and turrets look right in 3D and a sprite of them would not. Two of the weapon families carry an element, poison or fire, and a run commits to one of them (see Elements, below).

Elements: poison and fire

Poison is a debuff creatures carry: they turn bright green and take a tick of damage every two seconds, with a green-white flicker and a puff so it is never quiet, and only a nudge of knockback. A poisoned creature keeps one entry per item: the same item hitting again resets the clock instead of stacking, a different poison item adds its own. Levelling a poison item raises its tick damage and, at a couple of levels, adds a stack; never the speed. The base pace is deliberate: a saw's worth of damage takes a poison ten seconds. Poison weapons prefer creatures that are not poisoned yet, so the debuff spreads instead of piling up on one goblin.

v0.8 · fire, the design

Fire is poison's loud cousin. Where poison is patient (a small tick every two seconds for ten seconds), fire is a burst: a creature that catches fire takes 4 damage every 0.6 seconds for 1.8 seconds, three ticks and done, 12 damage in all against poison's 15. Hotter per second, gone sooner, worth less on one body. Its worth is in the crowd: every tick, every burning creature rolls to set alight each creature it is touching (touching means the two bodies' radii plus a hand's width). A fire lit by a weapon jumps with the weapon's fire_spread chance, 50% at level one; a fire caught from another creature is a child fire and jumps at 40% of that, so 20%, and so do its children, so a pack goes up like a fuse and then peters out at the edges. A child fire never jumps back to the creature it came from, so no pair of goblins keeps each other burning; the fire has to find new bodies or die. Bosses do not catch fire from a neighbour (they can be lit directly).

The rules match poison's where it matters. One entry per item on a creature: the same item hitting a burning creature resets its clock instead of stacking; a second fire item adds its own. Levelling a fire item raises its tick damage and, at a couple of levels, its spread chance or its burn time; never the tick rate. Fire weapons aim at creatures that are not burning yet (nearest unburnt, thickest unburnt crowd), so the flames go where there is something left to burn.

You cannot wield both. A run commits to one element the moment it holds a poison or fire item, weapon or passive. From then on the level-up cards, the travelling shop and the reroll never offer the other element; the chest reel only ever levels what you hold, so it cannot cross either. The starter pick comes before the commitment, so a run can open with a Flare Gun and never see a Rattlesnake, or the other way round. Each item carries its element in its data (element on a passive, derived from fire_damage / poison_damage on a weapon) and Run.element_allowed is the one gate.

How it looks. A burning creature turns ember red and flickers, licks of orange and yellow flame rise from it the whole time it burns, each damage tick flashes it orange (poison's tick is green, a plain hit white), and catching fire pops a small flare with a ring of sparks and a match-strike sound. The Molotov's pool is a draped orange disc with flames that lick up and restart at the ground.

The items. Three weapons, one passive and three evolutions, mirroring poison's set so the two families are the same shape and the choice is about feel: Flare Gun (nearest unburnt, the Peashooter's slot in a fire build), Molotov (a fire pool, the Lob Grenade's slot), Branding Iron (a burning orbit, the Rattlesnake's slot), Kindling (+15% burn damage per level on every fire item, pairs with the Flare Gun), and Roman Candle, Firestorm and Ring of Fire as the evolutions (six damage a tick, longer burns, 70% spread). Numbers are in the table above and in content/weapons; the engine side is one debuff next to poison in EnemyManager (ignite, _tick_fire), the elemental cloud both bombs share, and the orange branch of the flash in the billboard shader.

Why this shape. Poison rewards spreading it thin and waiting; fire rewards herding. A player who can bunch a pack before the flare lands gets the whole pack for one shot, and a player who cannot gets a few goblins and a lesson. The two builds should feel like different games on the same screen, and the no-mixing rule is what keeps them from collapsing into "all debuffs on everything".

Evolutions

A weapon at level 8 with its paired passive at level 1 or more evolves at the next chest: the reel lands on the evolved form, and Take it swaps the weapon out. The evolved form gets a gold-trimmed mesh and cannot level further. One recipe per weapon, thirteen in all, listed in the weapon table above.

Level-up cards

  • Pool. Weapons not yet owned while a weapon slot is free, plus any owned weapon or passive below max level. Nothing outside the pool can appear.
  • Three cards. Luck adds a chance of a fourth. Rarity weights favour upgrades to items you already own so builds converge.
  • Reroll, skip, banish. Per-run charges bought in the shop. Skip pays ten gold so it is never a dead choice. Banish removes an item from this run's pool.
  • Card text is generated from data. The description is built from the item's effect list, so a new item never needs hand-written card copy unless we want flavour. The same generator feeds the pause screen, the collection and the chest reel.

Stats every effect can touch

Player stats: max_hp, armor, regen, move_speed, might, cooldown, area, projectile_speed, duration, amount, magnet, luck, greed, revives, rerolls, skips, banishes. Weapon stats: damage, cooldown, amount, pierce, area, speed, range, duration, knockback, chains, poison_damage, poison_stacks, poison_duration, fire_damage, fire_duration, fire_spread. Any effect names a stat by string, so adding a stat is adding a key to a list, and the pause screen lists whatever keys exist.

09

Creatures & waves

Seven regular creatures, four elite variants, the Elite and a boss, each a data file that picks a brain, a sprite set, stats and a drop table. Two dozen are alive from the first minute and sixty by the end (the engine still handles hundreds), so every creature is cheap: a billboard in a MultiMesh, a position in an array, and a brain that is a few lines of steering.

CreatureBrainNumbersRole
Goblinfrom 0:00 · Green. Greedy. Many.chase12 hp · 1.8 m/s · 6 dmg · packs of 3The crowd. Every spawn rolls its size, speed and a tint from a palette; a few come out as specials: bigger, tougher, red-tinted, worth more XP.

Arrives before the cactus so the second minute already has speed in it. (It replaced a coyote that came out looking like a fox.)

Its shots leave a faint green trail that fades over a second and a half, so the line back to the thrower is always on the ground. Forces movement.

Bull Beetlefrom 4:00 · One horn. Zero patience.charge70 hp · 1.35 m/s · 16 dmg · 9 m/s chargeThe brute. Winds up for 0.8 s with a red line on the ground, then charges along that line: the line is a promise, so moving off it is the dodge. Big gem drop, one chest in 33.
Elite variantsevery 90 s from 3:30base brain1.4–1.6× sizeAny roster creature with a modifier: shielded (armor 4, double HP) speedy (+70% speed) splitter (splits into four) explosive (a telegraphed blast on death). Glowing outline, four times the XP, always a chest.
Dune Scorpionthe Elite · 2:30 · 7:30 · 12:30charge260 hp (×1.8 per stage) · 18 dmg · 11 m/s charge · 3× sizeHalf a boss. All of the attitude. Appears near the hero with a toast, no intro, no bar; the edge pointer shows where it went. Long charges from 8 m out, all eight directions painted. Always a chest.
The Tumbleweed Kingboss · 5:00 · 10:00 · 15:00boss900 hp (×2 per stage) · 20 dmg · 5× sizeRolling charge with a telegraph line, a ring of goblins, a bounce slam with a shockwave ring. HP bar under the top band, a chest where it dies.

Reading a charge

A charger's wind-up only warns you if you can see where it points. The Bull Beetle and the Dune Scorpion carry side, back-diagonal and front-diagonal sets besides front and back (stills edited from the front painting, a walk clip each), and while winding up or charging they face their charge direction rather than their drift. The charge direction is fixed the instant the red line appears and the creature runs that line even if the hero has moved: the telegraph is what makes the dodge fair. Any creature gets eight directions by setting "directions": 8 in its JSON.

Wave director

  • Live cap. Starts at 25, grows three a minute and jumps twelve per stage, to a ceiling of 60. Swarm rings temporarily ignore the cap up to a hard limit of 80.
  • Roster. The timeline says which creatures are eligible at a given time and with what weights. The director rolls from that roster whenever the cap has room, spawning in bursts so packs arrive together.
  • Scaling. Creature HP grows with elapsed time (+10% a minute, compounding gently), then HP and damage jump with the stage multiplier (×1.8, ×2.8) and speed rises 10% a stage. Endless adds 10% a minute on top.
  • Scripted events. The Elite, elite variants, swarm rings and bosses are timestamped entries in the map's timeline.
  • Culling. Creatures more than 30 m behind the hero are teleported back onto the spawn ring ahead. Nothing is wasted, and the pressure stays in front. The boss and the Elite are never culled.
  • Crowd behaviour. Separation steering on a spatial grid so sixty goblins flow around cacti and each other instead of stacking into one sprite.
10

XP & levelling

Creatures drop gems, the hero walks over them, the bar fills, three cards appear. The cadence is a level-up every 20 to 30 seconds early and every 40 to 60 seconds late; the XP Beacon and the reel add a few levels outside the curve.

XP table, levels 1 to 40
gems
Small (1 xp), medium (5), large (25), scaled by the creature's xp_mult and by four for elite variants. 3D gem meshes that spin. Drop table per creature. The beetle, the mummy and the Elite drop large.
magnet
Base pickup radius 1.5 m. Gems inside it fly to the hero. The Magnet passive, the shop and Astro's trait raise it.
gem merging
When too many gems sit on the ground, the oldest merge into one bigger gem, the Vampire Survivors trick that keeps performance flat with a hundred kills a minute.
vacuum
A rare drop from elite variants collects every gem on the map; the Magnet Pulse pickup and the Uber Magnet structure do the same on purpose. The best feeling in the genre.
feedback
Gems collected within a quarter second are batched into one rising "+N XP" label and the bar pops, so a sweep through a field reads as one reward.
gold
Separate from XP. 3D coins drop rarely (a goblin one time in fifty), bosses spill a dozen, the Loot Cache gives 40, a sold chest a few, and greed scales it. Gold is spent at the travelling shop inside a run and in the permanent shop outside it.
11

Run start & first play

The hero starts every run with no weapon and picks one. That first choice is the run's opening move, and on the very first run it doubles as the tutorial.

The starter pick, every run

when
Immediately after GO, before the timer starts. The arena is visible behind the cards, empty, so the player sees where they are.
what
Three weapon cards from the unlocked weapon pool. No reroll, no skip. The chosen weapon enters slot 1 at level 1. Reference: Brotato's starting weapon choice.
character bias
Each hero has a favourite weapon that is always one of the three and gets a bonus when chosen. Heroes do not lock you into it.
why
It gives a decision before the first level-up, it makes heroes flavour rather than a fixed opener, and it teaches the weapon list one card at a time.

The very first run

  1. Title screen. One big PLAY. Shop, collection and settings are visible but quiet. Astro and Dry Gulch are preselected.
  2. Starter pick, fixed. The first offer is always Peashooter, Boomstick and Orbit Saws, because the three teach the three targeting styles: nearest, forward, orbit.
  3. Touch and drag. A hint panel says "TOUCH and DRAG anywhere below to move", then "Drag in any direction. Lift to stop." once the hero has moved.
  4. Walk over gems. "Walk over GEMS to level up" after the first kill. Cleared on pickup.
  5. Level up. The first card screen carries a one-line explainer per card type, weapon versus passive.
  6. Pause exists. At 1:30, a toast: "Tap the top bar any time to pause and see your build". Nothing else interrupts the run again.

Every hint is skippable by tapping, appears once, and can be reset from settings. The run itself is the tutorial; the chest reel and the structures explain themselves by being watched.

12

Menus & pause

Four screens outside the run and four overlays inside it (level-up, pause, the chest reel, the travelling shop). Pause matters most: at any moment the player can read exactly what every weapon, passive and stat is doing, in words and numbers, not icons.

Look. Survivor.io is the target, and the whole look is one small file, ui/UiKit.gd. Navy panels with a lighter blue rim, one gold for the thing to press, purple for XP and passives, green for good news, red for danger. Headers, numbers and buttons are set in Lilita One, body text in Baloo 2 (both OFL, in ui/fonts); anything over the world gets a dark outline. Buttons carry a soft shadow and a darker bottom edge so they read as physical; primary buttons are white on gold with a brown rim.

Cards that cannot overflow. Every tappable card is a TapCard: a panel that sizes itself to its content (icon left, text column right, generous padding) and fires pressed once per tap, on touch or mouse, giving the tap up when the list starts scrolling. Icons are always square and mouse-transparent, so a tap on the picture is a tap on the card. Every overlay anchors its header, its scrolling list and its buttons to the screen as three bands, so a long list can never push the buttons off the bottom.

UI kit

BGBG2BG3LINEACCENTXPGOODDANGERINFO

Everything above is drawn by code (StyleBoxFlat), which is why it stays coherent: one palette, two fonts, one factory for every box. When the look should become painted art, Godot's StyleBoxTexture stretches a painted button or panel by its nine slices, and tools/gen_ui.py can paint such a sheet on the art server (untested against it so far). Layout, sizes, motion and the palette stay code either way.

Motion. Nothing appears, everything arrives: overlays fade in while their panel slides up 40 px, the three level-up cards stagger in, the reel decelerates and bounces, toasts and the boss bar scale in, every button squashes while held, the picked card punches before the screen closes, hub lists stagger their rows, and every scene change cross-fades through black (ui/UiFx.gd, all tweens, all under 0.3 s so the thumb never waits).

Pause screen, all three tabs

build
Every weapon and passive held, expandable. Each shows: icon, name, level, plain-language description, live numbers for every stat it has, damage dealt and kills this run, what the next level adds, and evolution status with the missing piece named.
stats
Every player stat as a row with its full breakdown: base, hero trait, shop tiers, passives, timed buffs, and total. No stat is hidden.
options
Camera mode, joystick size, screen shake, sound and music volume, reset hints, debug panel, abandon run.
entry
The round pause button, or a tap anywhere on the HUD strip. The game freezes instantly, including sound. Backgrounding the app pauses it too.

PLAY, the current pick chip, Shop, Collection, Settings. Gold and best run at the top. Background is the live Dry Gulch skybox.

PLAY → play setup: hero cards (portrait, trait, favourite weapon, quest text if locked) and the map card on one screen → GO → starter pick → run. Two taps if you keep the last choice, because the chip remembers it.

Megabonk's loop between runs: gold buys permanent stats, and in-run challenges unlock heroes, weapons and modes. Small but complete, because "do I want another run" is half the test.

Heroes

A hero is a trait plus a favourite weapon. The favourite is always in the starter offer and gets a bonus if picked, so heroes flavour a run without dictating it. Every hero's icon is a painted close-up doing something (the Drifter tips his hat, Astro gives a thumbs-up with a planet in her visor, Dad a double thumbs-up), made as an edit of the hero's own front still and set into a round badge that fills the plate.

14

Content is data, in Godot

The one architectural rule: content is both a data file and something you open, see and tweak inside the Godot editor. In Godot those are the same thing.

The rule

A new weapon, passive, evolution, creature, elite variant, hero, structure, pickup, shop upgrade, quest, sound or wave timeline is a new content folder and nothing else. It appears in the game the moment the folder exists. Code changes are allowed only to add a brand-new behaviour primitive that no existing file could express, and that primitive must then be reusable by any future content.

Test for every content addition: could Garry make this in the Godot editor, without asking Claude? If not, the system is wrong, not the content.

How it looks in the editor

Godot's own resource format is the data format. A custom Resource class with exported fields shows up in the Inspector as a form: sliders for numbers, dropdowns for enums like targeting, file pickers for the icon and the visual scene, and an "Add element" button for the effect list. Each content item is a folder:

FileWhat it holdsHow you edit it
boomstick.jsonThe authoring source: stats, level table, targeting, pairing, rarity, the art prompt.Edit the text, press "JSON → .tres" in the Content dock (or run import_json.gd).
boomstick.tresThe same numbers as a Godot resource.Click it, edit in the Inspector. Sliders and dropdowns, no code.
boomstick_visual.tscnWhat it looks like in the world: the shotgun mesh (Held), the pellet (Projectile), the muzzle point; the Peashooter's pod is a Familiar node the same way.Open it in the 3D editor, move things, swap the mesh, press play to preview.
boomstick_icon.pngThe icon used by cards, the HUD, pause, the reel and the collection.Replace the file, or re-run gen_art.py --only boomstick.

Creatures follow the same shape: goblin.json for stats, brain choice, drops (including its chest chance), the variance block and how many directions it is painted from; goblin_sprite.png is the strip. A map is a folder with its arena scene, its wave timeline (roster, events, pickups, structures), its music and its creature list.

The Content dock

A small editor plugin adds a "Content" panel to Godot. It lists every item by type with its icon, warns about missing files, and has "New from template" per type: it duplicates a template folder and renames the id. "JSON → .tres" regenerates the resources. A Test button launches the game with that item already equipped, so a change is playable in ten seconds.

The same weapon as JSON

// res://content/weapons/boomstick/boomstick.json
{
  "id": "boomstick", "name": "Boomstick", "rarity": "common",
  "behavior": "ProjectileEmitter", "targeting": "forward",
  "base": { "damage": 6, "cooldown": 1.4, "amount": 5, "spread_deg": 35, "range": 6, "pierce": 0, "knockback": 8, "speed": 16 },
  "levels": [
    [],                                                       // lv1 = base
    [{ "stat": "amount",   "op": "add", "value": 1 }],      // lv2
    [{ "stat": "damage",   "op": "mul", "value": 0.2 }],    // lv3
    // … to lv8
  ],
  "sfx": { "fire": "w_boom_fire", "hit": "w_boom_hit" },
  "evolves_with": "might", "evolves_into": "doomstick",
  "art_prompt": "a chunky double-barrelled shotgun…"
}

Where the line is

data only
New weapon using an existing behaviour (poison or fire included: the element is a few stats). New passive. New evolution. New creature using an existing brain (chase, flock, kite, charge, boss). New elite variant. New hero. New structure with an existing effect. New pickup. New shop tier. New quest with an existing condition type. New wave timeline. New sound assignment. New icon.
needs code
A behaviour that does not exist yet, such as a boomerang. A brain that does not exist yet, such as a burrower. A structure effect that does not exist yet. A quest condition type that does not exist yet. Each is built once as a reusable primitive with exported parameters.
never code
Card text, icons, balance numbers, pairing recipes, rarity, chest odds, unlock conditions using existing checks, which mesh a weapon uses, which sound plays.
15

Art

Clean anime. Heroes and creatures are cel-shaded sprites, painted once per view by an image model and set in motion by a video model, so they move like drawings and stay the same character from every direction. Everything they touch, throw, orbit, pick up or stand on is 3D. Icons are one bold object each with a black outline, made to read at 72 px on a phone. All of it is generated on the local art server from prompts that live in the content files.

What is 3D and what is a sprite

ThingMade asWhy
Heroes, creatures, bosses2.5D sprite camera-facing billboard pivoting on the feet, five painted views, mirrored to eight directionsPainted faces read better than low-poly ones, and a view per direction keeps the character honest from the high camera.
Weapons, familiars and their effects3D mesh + particlesSaw blades on a tilted orbit, a grenade on a real arc, a pea pod with flapping leaves. Sprites of these would look flat and wrong from above.
Pickups: gems, coins, chests, power-ups3D mesh spinning; power-ups a billboard icon on a plinthCheap, readable from any angle, hundreds on screen through a MultiMesh.
Terrain, landmarks, structures, skybox3D low-poly, paintedThe ground is 3D by definition; the big landmarks and the structures come from Blender.
Scenery: cacti, rocks, bones, dead trees, signs2.5D sprite one painting each, base-pivot billboards in a MultiMeshThey match the cast's line, cost one draw call per kind, and hundreds of them scatter for nothing. Muted so they read as background.
Telegraphs, progress wedges, poison clouds, spit trailsdraped meshes on the groundThey must hug dunes and mesa edges; a flat disc cuts through a slope.
Icons, cards, HUD, menus2DScreen-space UI.
Shadows under characters3D blobGrounds a flat sprite in a 3D world. The single most important trick for 2.5D.

The hero's sprite never holds a weapon. Weapons float at marker points around the character: a hip point for the shotgun, a ring for the saws, an orbit for the pea pod and the dart. That keeps the sprite one image per pose and lets any weapon pair with any hero.

Sprite animation

Heroes are pose-driven. A Mixamo motion (a run, a pain gesture) is rendered as an OpenPose skeleton with hands from each of the five game views in Blender (tools/pose_driver.py), and Wan 2.2 Animate moves the painted still along it. Every driver frame is a sprite frame: 24 frames per stride at 36 fps, frame rates carried in the hero's JSON. Animate paints the body on the driver's nose-to-ankle skeleton, which came out about a head taller than the painted still, so every animated frame is measured and fitted to the standing figure's height before it is packed; idle, run and hit now share one head height. The method, with before-and-after clips of the Drifter, has its own page.

The hit reaction is painted, not driven. The Mixamo pain gesture never looked right on any hero, so the hurt pose is a still per view: the image model edits the view's own painting into a flinch (leaning back, shoulders hunched, a hand to the chest, and for Astro the visor kept opaque), it is fitted to the standing height, and four frames at 12 fps wince around it (the flinch, a deeper lean, the flinch, half a step back to standing). It reads like the rest of the sheet because it is made the same way.

Creatures use free clips. Ants, cacti, beetles, mummies and the tumbleweed have no human skeleton, so their front and back stills are asked to walk in place by Wan 2.2 image-to-video, the loop is found by comparing silhouettes and twelve frames are cut at 15 fps. Chargers get three more stills (side, both diagonals, edited from the front painting) and a clip each. The goblin family and the mummy could move to the humanoid drivers later.

AnimationHeroCreatureTrigger
idle4 per view4 front + 4 backnot moving
run24 per view · 36 fps12 front + 12 back · 15 fps (chargers: five views)moving; the back set while walking away from the camera
hit4 per view · 12 fps (a painted flinch + a wince)1took damage
attack—2winding up a spit or a charge (chargers hold their directional idle instead)
die11HP zero, then pop
cheer1—extract, results

Procedural layer on top, no frames needed: bob while moving, lean into turns, scale-pop on spawn, squash on hit with a white flash (green-white when the hit is poison), a green tint while poisoned, wobble when tossed, shrink on death, and a shadow that shrinks with height. These come from the shader and a few lines of code. Strips are grids (strip_cols in the JSON, read by both billboard shaders): a hero strip is 153 cells of 256 px, a charger's 83 cells of 192.

Painted scenery, and reading through it

How they sit in the world. Each prop is an instance in one MultiMesh per sprite (core/systems/PropField.gd), a quad pivoting on its base that faces the camera exactly like the creatures do (prop_billboard.gdshader). Props and characters are both drawn opaque with an alpha cut rather than blended, so the depth buffer sorts them per pixel: a goblin standing in front of a cactus covers it, one behind it is covered, and because every quad is tilted the same way towards the lens the planes are parallel and never cut through each other, so there is no z-fighting to manage. Greenery sways a few degrees at the top in the vertex shader; rocks and bones do not.

Pipeline

  1. Prompt. Every content JSON carries an art_prompt (and heroes a portrait_prompt, anim_hint and anim_negative). The script wraps it in the house style.
  2. Stills. ComfyUI on the R9700 server runs Flux.2 Klein 9B (4 steps, about 20 s a render): a front view for everything, then a back view (and for heroes and chargers a side and two diagonals) edited from the front so the character stays the same.
  3. Motion. Heroes: pose drivers into Wan 2.2 Animate (about a minute a clip). Creatures: Wan 2.2 image-to-video, the loop period found from silhouettes (about two minutes a clip).
  4. Check. LM Studio's vision model grades every render (one subject, not cropped, no text, flat background, right view) and failures re-roll with a new seed up to three times; the grade is kept in <id>_ai.json.
  5. Cut. Key the green screen, drop specks and ground shadows, lift contrast, add the outline (heavier on creatures than on heroes), fit the cell, pack the grid strip, write the frame counts and rates back into the JSON. Hero portraits are cropped from an edit of the front still and set in a round badge.
  6. Review. tools/dl/review/ gets an icon sheet, a strip sheet and every sprite at its on-screen size on the sand texture.
  7. Scenery. tools/gen_props.py paints the fourteen props from the anchor, keys, outlines thinly, mutes and writes art/sprites/props/props.json with each prop's height and collider radius; the map reads that manifest. Landmarks are modelled in Blender by script and exported as GLB; textures for sand, cracked earth, sandstone and the sky panorama are generated by tools/gen_textures.py.

One creature costs about six minutes of server time; a charger about fifteen; a hero about twenty. python tools/gen_art.py --only coyote does the whole thing and imports the result into Godot.

16

Sound

Cartoon western: boings, splats and twangs, with a galloping soundtrack that adds a layer per stage. Every sound has an id that content files reference, a trigger, and a description written as a prompt for a sound AI. Placeholders are synthesised by script so the game is never silent while we wait for the real ones.

direction
Nothing realistic. Hits are "bonk" and "splat", deaths are comedic, UI is wooden and warm. Saturday-morning cartoon foley over a spaghetti-western guitar.
mixing rules
Voice limits per id, so forty fire ants dying is one sound with a pitch spread. Player and UI always audible. Creature sounds attenuate with distance from the camera. Everything ducks under the level-up sting.
placeholders
tools/gen_sfx.py writes a short WAV for every id: blips for UI, filtered noise bursts for hits, pitch sweeps for jumps and pickups, a looped chord for music. Ugly, but correct in timing and volume, and the sound map already points at the right ids. Voice barks come from Kokoro TTS.
music
Three run layers that come in per stage, a boss track, a title track, results; generated by tools/gen_music.py.

17

Tech & performance budgets

engine
Godot 4.7.2, GDScript. Compatibility renderer for the widest Android reach.
targets
Android first, on Garry's phone through a signed release APK dropped in Google Drive. PC for testing with WASD. 60 fps on a mid-range phone.
creatures
Budget of 60 alive by the end of a run (25 at the start), hard cap 80 during swarm rings; the arrays and MultiMeshes are sized for 320, so the cap is a design number, not an engine one. Logic is data-oriented: positions, velocities, HP, poison sources and frame index live in packed arrays, not one node per creature. Rendering is one MultiMeshInstance3D per creature type, billboarded in a shared shader, with the animation frame, flip, flash and squash as per-instance custom data.
movement
Creatures are not physics bodies. Separation steering on a spatial hash grid, updated every other physics tick. The hero is one CharacterBody3D against terrain and static prop colliders.
effects
Every burst, puff, flame, spark and flash is an instance in one of two pooled MultiMeshes (400 particles, two draw calls, no nodes). Point lights on chests, structures and pickups are skipped on phones, where every lit pixel pays for each of them; the campfire and the portal keep theirs. Phones render the 3D view at 80% and the UI at full size.
projectiles
Object pooled 3D meshes, 400 of them. Straight shots hold their muzzle height above the ground wherever they go; arcs ignore contact and explode where they land. Hit checks are sphere tests against the same grid, not physics queries. Hostile shots drop a fading trail dot every 55 ms into a second pool.
scenery
Painted props are MultiMesh billboards (one per sprite kind, up to 200 instances each), opaque with an alpha cut so they depth-sort against creatures per pixel; the occluded-outline pass on creatures and the hero is a second material with an inverted depth test.
sprites
Every sprite faces the camera fully (a quad pivoting on its feet, tilted towards the lens), so nothing is seen edge-on from the high camera. The hero is one quad with the sprite_billboard shader; creatures use the MultiMesh twin with the same maths. Both read grid strips.
ground marks
Telegraph rings, lines, sectors, the poison cloud's disc and the structures' progress wedge are meshes built on the map's height_at, so they drape over dunes instead of cutting them.
terrain
One heightmap mesh, 140 m, with a height-blended two-texture shader. Collision from the heightmap. Mesas and ramps are separate modular meshes and report their own height.
save
One JSON save file: gold, shop tiers, unlocks, quest progress, settings, best runs, hint flags, one-time migrations.
audio
A sound map resource binds every id from section 16 to a file. Voice-limited pools per id.
testing
A parse check of every script and scene, 33 gdUnit4 tests, a perf mode of the smoke run (perf=1) that prints each system's milliseconds per frame and every frame over 33 ms with what it was doing, a headless smoke run that plays through two bosses, every structure, the reel, the Elite and every hub screen, and a silent screenshot pass that captures every screen for this document. bash tools/ship.sh runs the checks, builds the signed APK and drops it in Drive.
18

Where it stands

The five feel-test milestones are done and the game has been iterated from the phone since. What follows is the short history, so a reader knows why things are the way they are, and what is next.

  1. Tooling and desert greybox

    Godot, gdUnit4, adb, the project skills. Heightmap terrain with the riverbed and mesas, the three steering variants, auto-jump gaps, the first APK.

    Answered: hold-and-slide lost to the floating joystick; the fixed north-up camera won over the chase camera.

  2. First blood

    Starter pick, the first three weapons in 3D, goblins and ants through MultiMesh, gems, cards, pause with Build and Stats.

    Answered: auto-fire plus steering is fun with a crowd; hundreds of creatures were too many to read, dozens with variance are right.

  3. Full run

    Ten weapons with evolutions and passives, the wave timeline, elite variants, the Tumbleweed King, the portal, endless. The content pipeline and the Content dock.

    Answered: a 15-minute run holds; builds feel different; a weapon is a folder.

  4. Meta and menus

    Title, play setup, three heroes, shop with refund, quests, collection, results, first-run hints, save file, the Survivor.io UI kit.

  5. Art and sound

    The anime style anchor, Flux.2 Klein stills, Wan 2.2 cycles, then pose-driven hero cycles with hit reactions and painted portraits. Blender props. Placeholder sound, generated music and voice barks.

  6. Iterated from the phone (v0.5 to v0.7)

    Zoomed out camera. Pickups and timed buffs. Structures with the stand-to-use wedge and the travelling shop. Draped ground marks and terrain-hugging shots. Chargers in eight directions and charges that keep their telegraphed line. Poison, the Rattlesnake and Skull Rain reworked, the Poison Dart and its familiar, the Peashooter's pod. The chest reel with Take and Sell. Dust Mummy and the Dune Scorpion. Harder stages. The boss pointer. Spit trails. The meadow map shelved. Then (v0.8): fire as a second element with three weapons, a passive and three evolutions, and the one-element rule; the Roadrunner in place of a coyote nobody liked; hero frames fitted to one height; effects pooled and phone lights cut after fps drops in the first minutes; chests half as common from the crowd and a tap to hurry the reel. Then (v0.9): the desert's scenery repainted as 2.5D sprites with an outline for whoever stands behind them; the hero's bar moved into the world; the flinch painted; the Flare Gun given a body; a real shotgun; the camera a step further out; seven structures, more cacti and bones.

Next

  • Move the goblin family and the mummy to the humanoid pose drivers so their strides are as clean as the heroes'.
  • Real sound effects from the prompt column, and a painted UI skin from gen_ui.py once it has run against the server.
  • A second map as a content pack, once Dry Gulch is the game it should be.
19

Open questions

Decisions taken so the build could exist. Each is a one-line change if it turns out wrong.

  • Death ends the run. One life, a revive as a meta unlock.
  • The starter pick happens every run, not only on the first.
  • Weapons are 3D, characters are sprites. The hero never visibly holds a weapon in the sprite.
  • Creature cap 25 to 60. The engine keeps its 320 budget so the cap can go back up in data.
  • Chests pause the game. Four seconds of reel per chest is the price of making a chest an event; the regular-creature odds are set so a run sees a handful, not a dozen.
  • Selling a chest pays a fifth of the shop price. Deliberately small; if gold ever matters more inside a run, this is the first number to raise.
  • Fire spreads at a flat 40% of the weapon's chance for every generation after the first. A decaying chain (20%, 8%, 3%) was the alternative; the flat one keeps big packs exciting and is one constant to change.
  • The Elite is one creature per map. A second mini-boss with a different brain (a spitter, say) would be a folder and one more event line.
  • Game name. "88fits" is the folder name and the working title.

Open questions that only more playing can answer: whether stage 2 is now a wall or a cliff, whether the coyote pack needs a sound of its own to be read before it arrives, whether the reel should ever offer a new weapon instead of a level, and how long endless stays interesting past minute twenty.
